deep.reconstruction:
This page (folio 2v) has no mathematical derivation. It is the second page of Riemann's 'Selbstanzeige', the self-review of his memoir 'Beiträge zur Theorie der durch die Gauss'sche Reihe F(α,β,γ,x) darstellbaren Functionen'. The review was printed in the Göttinger Nachrichten, 1857, No. 1, and is reproduced in Riemann's Werke. The prose continues a sentence from the previous page about Euler's special transformation of the hypergeometric series.

Content, step by step:
(1) Euler found a special case of the transformations of F(α,β,γ,x) into similar series in an algebraic function of x. He treated it in the Institutiones calculi integralis and in several papers, most simply in Nova Acta Acad. Petrop. XII, p. 58. In modern terms this is Euler's transformation F(a,b;c;x) = (1-x)^{c-a-b} F(c-a,c-b;c;x). The closely related Pfaff transformation is F(a,b;c;x) = (1-x)^{-a} F(a,c-b;c;x/(x-1)).
(2) The relation was later proved in different ways by Pfaff (Disquisitiones analyticae, Helmstedt 1797), by Gudermann (Crelle's Journal 7, p. 306) and by Jacobi.
(3) Kummer (Crelle 15) developed Euler's method into a procedure that could in principle find all transformations, i.e. all algebraic substitutions x -> z(x) carrying solutions of the hypergeometric equation into solutions. Carrying it out required lengthy case discussions, so he did not complete the third-degree case. He fully derived only the transformations of degree 1 and 2 (the 24 Kummer solutions and the quadratic transformations) and their compositions.
(4) Riemann states that his memoir applies to these transcendents a method whose principle he had stated in his Inaugural Dissertation, Art. 20. That principle is that a many-valued function is determined, up to constants, by its branch points and its type of behaviour there. With it, all previously known results follow 'almost without computation'. He hopes to present further results obtained by the same method to the Society soon.

The next page shows Riemann starting the actual work. He writes the Euler integral ∫ y^α (1-y)^β (1-xy)^γ dy between any two of 0, 1, 1/x, ∞. He then maps four points a, b, c, d to ∞, 0, 1, 1/x by a Möbius map, which gives x as a cross-ratio. Nothing of that is on this page.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. Minor bibliographic point from the context: Kummer's memoir 'Über die hypergeometrische Reihe' is in Crelle 15, usually dated 1836. The previous page says 1835. This is a dating detail, not an error on this folio.
